text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- The world's most valuable stamp, Sweden's Treskilling Yellow, goes on sale in Zurich on Friday. It last sold in 1990 for nine million crown ($1.4 million).

- New listings in Stockholm this year have received a lot of interest, rising on average 55 percent. So far five new companies have listed on the bourse with another six expected by year end, including Pharmacia & Upjohn unit Biacore.

- Riksbank governor Urban Backstrom has criticised the Calmfors report on Sweden's and the European Union's single currency, saying it wrongly estimated the costs of joining EMU. The report recommended Sweden delay EMU membership. Backstrom said he saw no profit from staying outside the EMU.
- The Swedish Trade Union Federation (LO) is partly blamed for the nation's rising unemployment, pushing for higher wage increases every year for the past 25 years.

- A list of new, big orders, lifts telecom giant Ericsson's share price on the Stockholm bourse. This week Ericsson has announced a $280 million expanded deal in Guangdong, China, $400 million frame agreements with two other Chinese companies, and a $300 million agreement with U.S.'s AT&T.
- Swedish parliament has heated debate over Prime Minister Goran Persson's controversial comments on political stability in China during a visit to Beijing this week.
- Truck and bus maker Scania AB said third-quarter pre-tax profit fell a more-than-expected 94 percent because of extra costs in switching production to a new truck series and the stronger krona.

- Nordic stock exchanges, facing increased competition in Europe, may join together in a single holding company. The first stage in cooperation may be taken if the Stockholm Exchange mergers with OM, the derivates exchange operator. Head of Helsinki's exchange, Mika Bjorklund, said he was interested in discussing cooperation. Spokesmen from Oslo and Copenhagen said maintaining national stock listings but consolidating all trading in a single regional system may work.

- Swedish forestry group Sodra said there is a risk of a setback for pulp prices with producers unable to implement the price hike for softwood pulp of $620 a ton announced in September. Demand from Asia has slowed.
